item.title: I compressed my Steam library instead of buying another SSD, and got 400GB back
item.itunes:title: I compressed my Steam library instead of buying another SSD, and got 400GB back
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
With AAA titles taking up more than 100GB of storage space these days, even a 2TB SSD won't cut it unless you're okay with uninstalling and reinstalling games as you need them. For years, I never really had more than four or five games installed on my PC at any given time, so storage space wasn't something I was worried about. That changed after I installed three AAA games that took up about 150GB each and watched my SSD fill up quickly. At that point, it's impossible not to consider a secondary drive.

But over the last year, SSDs have become way more expensive, just like RAM, because of AI demand, with some mainstream drives costing nearly three times as much as they did a year ago. That's what convinced me to spend $6 on a compression tool that I randomly found on Steam. I didn't have any high expectations going into it, but it went on to free up hundreds of gigabytes of space, which was enough to stop me from even thinking about buying another SSD at these inflated prices for the time being.

SSD prices aren't coming down anytime soon, but used enterprise SSDs could be the answer you're looking for

Pre-owned enterprise SSDs are built to last, and they're quite cheap on eBay

By  Tanveer Singh

Some games gave me way more space than I expected

You can see exactly which games are actually worth compressing

The moment you open Game Compressor, you'll see all the games installed on your PC under the Game Library section of the dashboard, whether they're from Steam, Epic Games, Ubisoft Store, or Riot Client. And honestly, that immediately gave me a great first impression because I don't have to manually point it to each folder using File Explorer. To get started, click Scan in the top-right corner and wait for Game Compressor to analyze your library and show how much space you couldsave. It breaks down the potential savings for each game individually.

While that's already enough to know which games are worth compressing, I recommend clicking each game individually because you don't want to compress a game that uses DirectStorage. Those games may stutter or take longer to load after compression. Also, games with little compressible data will probably only save you MBs. Battlefield 6 is a good example in my case, showing only 0.3% potential savings for a 100GB installation. Compressing God of War, on the other hand, freed up about 25GB of space, even though it was only 64GB originally. I personally don't bother compressing games that show less than 5% potential savings.

This didn't change how I played my games

Games still run normally because decompression happens on the fly

At this point, you're probably wondering: why not just right-click on the game folder, go to Advanced, and choose Compress contents to save disk space? You can technically do that, but it can noticeably slow your games because it uses traditional NTFS compression (LZNT1). Game Compressor, on the other hand, uses Windows' LZX compression, which is better suited to files that are frequently read but rarely modified. And this compression happens at the file-system level, so the game can still access its files normally.

Yes, games that use DirectStorage risk performance regression because file-system compression can interfere with its optimized I/O path. For other games, this shouldn't be a concern as long as you have a relatively new CPU because the CPU does the decompression on the fly. At least in the games I tested with my 5800X3D and RTX 4090, performance and loading times were mostly similar. You can even update your games like you normally do and continue playing, but you can recompress them from the Updates section of Game Compressor.

I didn't have to spend $6 for this

But the other options aren't nearly as convenient

Game Compressor isn't some breakthrough tool, and LZX compression isn't exclusive to it. You can actually take advantage of it natively in Windows by simply using the compact.exe tool. The only problem is that you have to open Command Prompt and enter the appropriate commands every time you want to compress or decompress a game. CompactGUI makes this easier by giving you an interface. You just need to point it to the folder using File Explorer, choose LZX, and let the tool handle the rest.

But what these free methods lack is convenience. You have to compress each game one by one, whereas Game Compressor detects all your games automatically and gives you more context to help you decide which ones are worth compressing. I like that you can simply click Compress All and it'll automatically avoid compressing games that use DirectStorage. And let's not forget how it shows the ones that need recompression once you update your games. All these features easily make it worth the $6 I paid, considering how much I spend on Valorant skins these days.

That $6 stopped me from splurging on an SSD in today's market

I see my purchase as an absolute win all around. It doesn't even cost as much as an indie game, yet it helped me get back a ton of storage space. Of course, this isn't a replacement for an SSD, but now I have enough breathing room to wait until prices come down. So if you're on the fence about getting a secondary drive, see how much space you can free up with this tool first. You're not limited to compressing games either, as you can manually add any folder that's taking up a lot of space on your PC.

Game Compressor

Game Compressor is software that scans and compresses your game library to save storage space without impacting performance.

$5.99 at Steam
I put my Steam library on my NAS, and it was both brilliant and stupid

The best (or the worst, depending on how you see it) part? It works really well

By  Ayush Pande

item.title: Excel's new Copilot feature will turn your spreadsheets into interactive visuals, and they'll auto-update too
item.itunes:title: Excel's new Copilot feature will turn your spreadsheets into interactive visuals, and they'll auto-update too
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • An upcoming Copilot-powered Excel canvas feature turns workbook data into polished, interactive visuals.
  • Canvases auto-update with data changes, and you can edit them by chatting with Copilot.
  • Microsoft plans a broad rollout for desktop and web in September 2026 as per the AI at Work Roadmap.

Getting your data organised in Excel is one thing; making it look presentable is another. Fortunately, Microsoft has been adding some interesting new Copilot-powered features to the spreadsheet software that will make creating interactive canvases representing your data a lot easier. Best of all, it'll keep tabs on everything you change and automatically update the canvas as you work.

Microsoft's new "Excel canvas" feature makes creating and maintaining visual data a breeze

It should roll out to everyone sometime this month

You can see the details for yourself over on the AI at Work Roadmap. Microsoft has a few different roadmaps to keep businesses and consumers in the loop about what they can expect from future updates. The AI at Work one is, as you'd expect, a roadmap covering the implementation of new Copilot and AI tools.

This time, we're taking a look at Roadmap ID 569424: Excel canvas. It was added to the roadmap earlier this month, and reads like this:

A Copilot-generated canvas that turns workbook data into a polished, interactive view of key visualizations, metrics, and insights. As workbook data changes, it automatically updates to reflect the latest information. Users can modify the canvas by chatting with Copilot.

It sounds like a genuinely useful feature, especially the part where Excel will automatically update the visual as you make changes to the workbook. If done right, I can see it genuinely saving a lot of time and effort when creating interactive guides for your data.

Despite being marked as "In Development," Microsoft seems confident that they can get this new Excel canvas feature rolled out sometime in September 2026. When it does arrive, both desktop and web users can take advantage of this handy new feature.

Excel's Copilot finally tackles the nightmare of sorting through your open-ended survey data

Just a few clicks and you're done.

By  Simon Batt

item.title: I can't replace these 4 free Windows tools, and they are better than any paid alternative
item.itunes:title: I can't replace these 4 free Windows tools, and they are better than any paid alternative
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Over nearly 21 years of using Windows, and over 4 years of using Windows 11 as my daily driver, I've developed numerous habits on the OS, and a lot of my workflow relies on some valuable tools that Microsoft gives away for free.

If you, too, are using Windows 11 as your daily driver, chances are you've probably used these tools (and possibly, rely on them) without realizing they are available nowhere else. And if you haven't, I strongly recommend using these 4 tools to make the OS more powerful, convenient, and a lot more capable for your everyday tasks.

Snipping Tool

Windows 11's screenshot tool ruined every other tool for me

Perhaps the first time I realized the sheer value Windows 11's Snipping Tool brings me in the time I saved was when I was actually away from my main desktop. I have an old PC running Windows 10 and an M2 MacBook Air that I use whenever I'm away, and on both, taking a screenshot is surprisingly arduous and painful, to say nothing of whatever comes after in the editing phase.

On Windows 11, it's completely effortless with the Snipping Tool. Your screenshots are automatically saved to a dedicated Screenshots folder by default, but that's only the beginning. A lot of users like to describe Snipping Tool as a productivity suite in itself, and they're not wrong. It has gotten considerably better over time, with OCR, screen recording capabilities, QR code detection, a color picker, and quick editing tools for highlighting, marking up, and adding shapes.

Most other operating systems' built-in screenshot tools pale in comparison, often forcing ou to introduce another step just to do something as simple as editing what you've captured. Microsoft absolutely nailed it with this one.

These built-in Windows apps improved my productivity, and I never expected them to be this good

Windows has decent built-in apps, so you don't need to install third-party software.

By  Brian Burgess

Windows Sandbox

It makes virtualization look like child's play

Windows Sandbox is one feature that I've written countless times about, and every time that I do, I seem to have a new use-case for it. I often find myself going straight to it without even realizing that Microsoft has been giving me this incredibly useful tool for free all along.

It does exactly what the name suggests, in that, it gives you a disposable Windows environment where you can tinker, test, and wreck things without worrying about consequences.

As such, all dubious GitHub scripts, suspicious attachments, malware-ridden dodgy executables are all thrown into the Sandbox first, because I'm assured that I can just close the window and leave the mess behind without ever having to think about nuking my Windows installation. There isn't really an equivalent one-click, throwaway desktop environment built into macOS or Linux, which makes it an absurdly good freebie.

Windows Sandbox is only available on Windows 11 Pro, Enterprise, and Education editions.

7 alternatives to built-in Windows tools that will blow you away

You don't need to rely on built-in Windows apps; here are alternatives that will do a far better job.

5
By  Brian Burgess

Photos

It has become good enough for me to not need anything else

It might seem like I am competing for contrarian Olympics with this one, but Microsoft's Photos app is something that I've unironically come to love. I've reached the point in my workflow where I almost never need another photo editor for 99% of what I do. It comes with Generative Erase now, which means I don't have to wait 20 years to wait for Adobe Photoshop to open just to get rid of a speck of dust on a product image.

Like everything else so far on this list, it's also one of the apps Microsoft has continually improved based on loud user feedback. You can access your OneDrive photos, import images from connected devices, and even remove backgrounds and save the results, which has saved me from paying for a one-off charge to an online utility to do the same thing.

5 window managers that make multitasking easier on Windows

You don't have to settle for Snap Layout

2
By  Anurag Singh

The PowerToys Suite

Need I say more?

At this point, if you haven't heard of or used at least one PowerToys utility on your Windows 11 PC, then that's a problem that you have to take care of straight away, possibly right now.

The PowerToys Suite is a collection of utilities that have single-handedly made Windows 11 an infinitely better OS than it could ever have been on its own, and I am confident that there is something of value to be found in this massive, almost ridiculous collection of tools for practically every single user.

It's not even possible for me to list every tool in its ever-expanding suite without this article reading like a full-length novel, so I'll go with the ones that I personally cannot imagine using the OS without.

First and foremost, FancyZones, because it seems like one of the utilities that brought PowerToys to wide renown. It takes Windows' default tiling management and makes it better by letting you customize grid layouts for each apps, so no app gets more desktop real estate than it realistically needs (who wants PowerShell to take up half your screen while coding?).

The next one is a personal favorite, because it made me stop using Windows Search, for which I never really had anything good to say about. The utility, of course, is Command Palette, which gets rid of everything you don't need in a search tool (like ads and news feeds and search engine results for your files) and can be run entirely using your keyboard.

If you're just starting out with PowerToys and use a lot of special characters, I'd heavily recommend Quick Accent, which made me stop Googling and pasting special characters like the degree symbol and also saved me from having to memorize obscure Alt codes. There's at least two dozen other utilities, and each improves your user experience in one way or the other. The beauty of it is you can choose to deploy them selectively.

Microsoft does a rather sloppy job in advertising some of the greatest tools it offers for users of Windows 11.

Windows has many gifts for the power user waiting to be discovered

When I say "waiting to be discovered", I absolutely mean that Microsoft does a rather sloppy job advertising some of the greatest tools it offers for users of Windows 11, and it really won't be a surprise if you discovered a utility (or an aspect, or a use-case of one) that you hadn't thought of before. For the right user, the desktop experience can be made a lot better, if only one remembers to look in the right places.

item.title: My Obsidian vault instantly got more useful when I started pairing it with these free apps
item.itunes:title: My Obsidian vault instantly got more useful when I started pairing it with these free apps
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Obsidian gets most of its praise from being local-first, offline, and future-proof with its plain-text nature. When you sit and think for a minute about what the vault actually is, a regular folder with markdown, then Obsidian suddenly becomes more than just a notes app and starts behaving more like a hub that other tools can plug straight into.

Community plugins get most of the attention when it comes to extending Obsidian, and there are thousands of good ones. But some of the most useful pairings live outside the app, in my opinion. And they work precisely because of the plain vault architecture. The free apps I want to talk about here all pair with the vault in slightly different ways for numerous use cases. And I reckon skipping them means missing out on what Obsidian's plugin ecosystem doesn't really give you.

If you're an Obsidian user looking to switch, try this open-source alternative

Is Notesnook the Obsidian alternative you have been waiting for?

2
By  Parth Shah

Obsidian Web Clipper

Bringing the web into my vault

First up is one of the most useful little gems I've stumbled across: Obsidian Web Clipper. It's an official free browser extension from the Obsidian team, and it works across Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge. It saves web pages as clean markdown, and you can pick between grabbing the entire page or just the main content depending on what you're clipping from. Templates are the other useful bit here, since you can set up per-site rules so the frontmatter fills itself in with things like source URL, author, and date automatically.

There's no middleware or sync service between them, all you have to do is tell the extension which vault folder to write to and every clip lands there as a markdown file. I have a dedicated Clippings folder in my vault for exactly this, and it's where anything I want to keep from the web ends up. So whenever something drops in, it's fully searchable and backlink-able in the vault, and also available in every other tool I've pointed at the vault. If you only try one of the tools from this article, this is the one I recommend grabbing.

4 ways to host Obsidian online

Turn your local Obsidian vault into an online knowledge hub — here’s how.

5
By  Dhruv Bhutani

Claude Desktop

The filesystem connector is free

Claude Desktop is Anthropic's free desktop app for Windows and macOS, and since February 2026, connectors and desktop extensions have been available on the free plan too. So although the paid Claude Code is a better setup for your vault, there's no paywall for this particular method. The filesystem connector is a one-click desktop extension that gives Claude read and write access to specific folders you nominate, so all you need to do is point it at your vault, and Claude treats it as regular folders and files.

I've had a Claude subscription for most of this year now, but before I did, this is actually how I made Claude talk to my vault. And the best use case is not even chatting, in my opinion, it's simply organization. My vault gets messy fast, but Claude can scan the whole thing, propose naming conventions or folder structures, and then also act on it if you give it write access.

One caveat is that moving or renaming files through the filesystem connector bypasses Obsidian's auto-link updates, so wikilinks will probably end up breaking. So this is best suited for raw notes that have not yet been structured and that you've been meaning to sort. Another downside is that the message limits on the free plan are tight, so this is best used as a focused pass rather than a long back-and-forth.

I turned Obsidian into a personal command center, and now I barely open separate apps

My notes, tasks, calendar, research, and writing finally live under one roof.

5
By  Patrick Hearn

AnythingLLM for local organization and querying

If you want to keep the whole pipeline local instead

I have multiple vaults, and only some of them get touched by cloud-based tools. But there are some that I keep entirely local because they contain more personal information, such as my medical and financial docs. So if you're looking for something similar to a Claude-Obsidian setup but want to keep the whole thing private, AnythingLLM is the way to go.

It's a fully local and self-hosted AI workspace that can plug right into your local LLM (I host my local LLM via LM Studio's server). AnythingLLM actually has a dedicated Obsidian data connector so you can pull in your vault folders and files in bulk and have them ready in the app to query. Just a note: lately I've been having issues with this connector, apparently it currently has a bug that doesn't let you pull in the files. But I can still manually add my vault contents through file upload too and utilize AnythingLLM's RAG system.

You can also use the File System Agent for write access, meaning you can organize the vault from within the app using natural language. But I just use AnythingLLM as a local chat layer on top of my vault to interrogate my own notes and research.

I tried replacing Notion with Obsidian as my main note-taking app and here’s how it went

The truth about switching from Notion to Obsidian

7
By  Parth Shah

Google Drive (and basically any Google app that integrates with Drive)

The most underrated and overlooked tool to use with your vault

Everyone knows what Google Drive is, so it doesn't need an introduction. But I think its use case is seriously underrated, especially among folks who prefer local setups. I understand not wanting to send all your data to Google servers, however, you have complete control over what you give it access to. Again, I have multiple vaults exactly for this purpose, one of which doesn't contain any revealing information, just random content and research.

My main Google tool is still NotebookLM, and it integrates directly with Google Drive. So the pipeline goes Obsidian vault -> sync with Drive -> fetch from Drive within NotebookLM. And here, I'm not even talking about chatting with my notes, I primarily use this setup because of NotebookLM's Mind Map feature. NotebookLM auto-builds a branching visual diagram of the concepts across my imported notes, and I can click any node to drill in further with a follow-up question.

Obsidian has manual mind-mapping options through plugins, but nothing that auto-populates from my existing notes the way NotebookLM does. So as a visual thinker, this setup is invaluable to me.

4 game-changing Obsidian workflows I wish I tried earlier

Obsidian workflows I tried late, but you don’t have to

4
By  Parth Shah

The vault is just a hub, not the whole setup

What all four pairings have in common is that they treat the vault as a folder of files rather than a closed app. You don't have to use all four though, honestly, but picking up just one will probably get you further than another handful of community plugins would. I don't like stuffing Obsidian with a bunch of plugins, anyway, so I get much more use out of my vault by pointing these tools at it.

item.title: I finally ran my Jellyfin library on my PlayStation 5, no matter how much Sony tried to stop me
item.itunes:title: I finally ran my Jellyfin library on my PlayStation 5, no matter how much Sony tried to stop me
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Ever since the PlayStation 5 came out, it has never had two things — a web browser and a Jellyfin client on the PlayStation Store. For as long as I've owned mine, I've settled with having to switch over to my TV's browser to access my Jellyfin library.

After completely shifting over from Plex and moving my entire media server to Jellyfin, I was in no mood to redo everything, and even though I have a perfectly good Jellyfin client in Wholphin, I decided that Sony would no longer get to dictate what I could use on my own PlayStation.

Filled with determination to stick it to the man, I decided I would find a way to access my Jellyfin library on my PS5 Pro, and a day later, I finally did. It's not the best way out there, and it definitely demanded its fair share of elbow grease, but boy was it thrilling to finally see my Jellyfin library on my PS5.

Jellyfin will never come to the PlayStation Store

The traditional methods don't work

There's never been an official Jellyfin app on the PlayStation Store. This is because Jellyfin has always been free and open-source software (FOSS). Sony, on the other hand, requires publishers looking to launch an app on the PS Store to sign NDAs and use closed-source SDKs, which runs counter to Jellyfin's open-source principles. There's always Plex on the PS5 app store, but I wasn't interested in rebuilding my entire Plex library from scratch or paying for Plex Pass.

On any other device, it would have been easy to open the web browser and type in my localhost URL to access my Jellyfin movies and shows, but the PlayStation makes something as simple as this excruciatingly frustrating. That's because the PS5 never shipped with a web browser, even though the PS4 did. The web browser was how many users jailbroke their PlayStation 4 consoles, so Sony decided to make things tougher for PS5 users by removing the web browser app altogether.

And yet, for four years, users simply opened a chat with their PS5 friends, typed in a link, and clicked on it to force-open the built-in browser. Sadly, Sony cracked down on that method in late 2024, sending TOS (terms of service) violation notifications to anyone who tried it. Clearly, Sony wasn't going to make it easy for me to access my Jellyfin library on my PlayStation 5, and the challenge involved genuinely had me excited to try.

item.title: I tested ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini on the same branding task, and only one felt ready for Instagram
item.itunes:title: I tested ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini on the same branding task, and only one felt ready for Instagram
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
My sister recently started making homemade chocolate chip cookies from her kitchen, and she wanted to turn that small idea into an actual business. The product was simple — one signature chocolate chip cookie. I thought the branding would be a fun test for AI. Instead of helping her myself, I decided to see what three popular AI chatbots would come up with.

I gave ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini the same job: build the brand from scratch, including the name, tagline, logo, colors, packaging, and social media launch content. I didn't give any of them extra instructions or change the prompt between tests. I wanted to see how differently they would interpret the exact same creative brief.

The exact prompt I gave all three AI chatbots 

You're helping launch a small home-based cookie business run by one person out of their home kitchen. They're known for one thing: a single, perfect chocolate chip cookie.
Create and produce the full brand kit:
Brand name — memorable, ownable, not generic
Tagline — one line that captures the whole vibe
Logo — Generates the logo as an image. It should suit the brand.
Color palette — 3–4 colors with names, hex codes, and the mood each sets
Packaging — generate an image showing how the cookie is wrapped or boxed
Social media launch post — write the first Instagram caption (with hashtags) and generate the accompanying photo which should match the brand identity
Make real choices — no hedging or multiple options. Produce every visual asset as an actual image, not just a description.

Models I used

  • ChatGPT GPT-5.6 Luna
  • Gemini 3.7 Flash
  • Claude Opus 4.8

Gemini was the fastest

Could have taken more time for better results

Gemini was the quickest of the three to finish the task. I didn't have to wait around for the complete response, which was nice when I was testing the same prompt across multiple tools. The speed, however, came with a few compromises.

The logo it created was basic, but I wouldn't call it bad, especially for a first attempt. The bigger issue was that Gemini somehow didn't attach the packaging image, even though I had specifically asked for one in the prompt. That made the final brand kit feel incomplete.

I also felt the color palette would have been easier to judge if Gemini had shown it visually instead of only listing the colors. The tagline was another weak point for me. It technically followed the instructions, but it read more like a regular sentence than a memorable brand tagline. Overall, Gemini got the job done quickly, but I felt it could have benefited from spending more time on the creative details.

I used Claude, Gemini, and ChatGPT to create my personal website, and there was a clear winner

The AI web dev battle.

10
By  Parth Shah

ChatGPT was the most creative

Creative enough!

ChatGPT was the one that impressed me the most creatively. The overall ideas felt more thought-out, and I genuinely liked the way it approached the visual side of the brand. The creatives looked polished enough to make the fictional cookie business feel like something I could actually imagine seeing online.

One thing that surprised me was that it could also create a background-removed version of the image. That wasn't something I expected to be particularly useful for this test, but it showed how flexible the image generation could be when working on a brand.

The biggest drawback was how it presented the visuals. Instead of giving me separate images for the logo, packaging, and social media, ChatGPT put several of them together in a single collage-style image. There were no individual assets, which was less convenient to use. It was a whole brand kit presented in a single image. Still, creatively, this was the response I enjoyed working with the most.

Claude was the slowest

Results could not justify the time

Claude took the longest to finish the task, and by the time the results were ready, I was expecting something that would really stand out. Unfortunately, the final output didn't quite match that expectation.

The logo was the first thing that caught my attention, and not in a good way. The elements felt like they were overlapping, which made the design look less clean than I wanted. It didn't have the same immediate visual appeal as the other results.

The social media post was another disappointment for me. It was extremely basic and didn't feel catchy enough for a brand trying to make its first impression on Instagram. The writing wasn't necessarily wrong, but it lacked the personality I was looking for.

I did like the color palette, though. It felt considered and suited the cookie brand well. The tagline was also decent and, like ChatGPT's, had a nice fit for the overall idea. But overall, the time it took didn't feel justified by the final result.

I made ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini summarize the same 200+ page PDF, and the results weren't even close

One prompt, one report, three very different approaches to summarizing a 200+ page document.

27
By  Yash Patel

The cookie was the same, but the brands weren't

This little experiment made one thing clear to me: creative AI isn't just about getting an answer, but about how each tool approaches an idea. I started with one simple cookie and ended up with three very different interpretations of the same business. For me, ChatGPT was clearly better than other tools. Sometimes, the best approach is to try the same idea in more than one place and see what clicks.

item.title: I disabled NAS drive sleep mode after watching the load-unload cycles destroy a $200 drive
item.itunes:title: I disabled NAS drive sleep mode after watching the load-unload cycles destroy a $200 drive
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When you set up a new NAS system, you might notice it constantly humming and drawing a lot of wattage, so you switch it to standby mode after 15 to 30 minutes of inactivity. This might feel like an energy-conscious decision, and you might notice your room get quieter, temperatures falling, and your annual electric bill dropping by up to $40.

However, 18 months later, a drive will drop from the pool with I/O errors. You pull the S.M.A.R.T telemetry logs and discover a horror show. The start-stop count and the load-unload cycle count have ballooned from a few hundred into the tens of thousands, accompanied by spindle spin retry errors and missing reallocated sectors.

Hard drive spin down is designed for single-drive desktop PCs, not multi-drive, container-dense home servers. The thermodynamic and mechanical stress of frequent spin-up cycles degrades spindle motors, head actuator ramps, and solder joints far faster than continuous rotation ever would. The money you've saved on electricity is quickly erased when you replace a $200 enterprise drive years ahead of its design life.

How long will a NAS last before needing to be replaced?

Planning for replacing your NAS and its hard drives is an important stage in your backup strategy.

5
By  Joe Rice-Jones

The physics behind the problem

The spinning plates cause some issues

  • Credit: 
  • Credit: 

Unfortunately, this issue is down to physics. When a 7,200 RPM mechanical drive is asleep, its platters are completely stationary. Switching it back on accelerates the high-density aluminum/glass platters to 7,200 RPM in just 8 to 15 seconds, which requires an initial inrush current surge of 1.5A to 2.5A on the 12V rail. This can be around 20 to 30W peak per drive. This creates extreme instantaneous torque stress on the fluid-dynamic spindle bearings and power-delivery components. Essentially, the spin-up surge is causing a mechanical shock to your hard drives.

Also, modern drives park their read/write heads on an external physical ramp off the edge of the platters when entering standby. Enterprise and NAS drives are rated for roughly 300,000 to 600,000 load/unload cycles; however, aggressive spin-down in a system triggered by frequent background tasks can blow through hundreds of cycles a week, essentially shortening the lifespan of your drive.

Thermal cycling can play a major role in the degradation of your drive too. Steady-state heat like 35 to 40°C is not what kills electronics. It's actually down to thermal delta: repeatedly cooling a drive down to an ambient 22°C during sleep and then rapidly heating it back up to 42°C during spin-up can cause microscopic expansion and contraction across the printed circuit board, solder joints, and drive casing, accelerating fatigue failures.

The worst are those who are running home labs

Home lab set-ups spin up more often than you think

An issue with a home lab drive is that I might not actually even be able to go to sleep. This is because of a constant wave of background pings. Even if you aren't actively streaming a movie or transferring a file, modern home servers are never truly idle. Plex/Jellyfin may run scheduled library metadata sweeps, Docker containers may write tiny log lines to shared storage pools, Home Assistant may record historical sensor states, or other status pings may keep your NAS constantly switching on and off.

This means that your drive can go to sleep after 20 minutes, but then 10 minutes later, an OS telemetry log or SMB broadcast wakes it up. It spins up for 90 seconds and then goes back to sleep. This thrashing loop causes issues with your drive's health. Instead of spinning down once or twice a night, the drives thrash through 15 to 30 spin-up cycles every single day.

The real-world annoyance of waiting 10 to 15 seconds with a frozen File Explorer or spinning client wheel, while storage already spins up from cold to standby, can also be an issue. You take a latency hit waiting for the drives to wake from sleep mode.

There might be a solution for you

And it likely isn't sleep mode

You can make a few compromises that let you save power without actually killing the disks.

Decouple Docker and app data onto flash storage like an NVMe or SATA SSD. Never let application data, container configurations, or OS system logs reside on your mechanical spinning array. Keep Home Assistant databases, Plex app data, and Docker configs strictly on dedicated cheap SSDs. That way you don't have to have your hard drive spin up so often.

Undergo the Unraid hybrid approach. In systems like Unraid, files are written directly to an NVMe cache pool and only flushed to spinning rust once a day in a single bulk batch at an allocated time, normally in the AM. This allows mechanical drives to sleep for 20+ hours uninterrupted, avoiding that thrashing.

Activate a 24/7 enterprise role if the other two options aren't for you. If you're running ZFS or traditional RAID, then it might be better for you to disable APM/spin down entirely. Disable drive standby in your GUI and let the drives spin continuously in a temperature-controlled chassis with adequate airflow. That way you don't have to worry about the health of your drives degrading from constant sleep cycles.

Your hard drives need to be cared for

This should save you from having to replace them prematurely

Hard drives are mechanical engines with spinning fluid bearings, voice coils, and floating heads. Like an automobile engine on a highway, hard drives are the happiest running at steady operating temperatures and constant speeds. Starting and stopping them 20 times a day to pinch pennies on power is textbook false economy. Go into your NAS settings today and audit your S.M.A.R.T load cycle counts. Turn off aggressive sleep timers, keep your drives spinning, and make your enterprise hardware do the job it was built to do.

item.title: AMD might finally be bringing its most important gaming CPU upgrade to laptops, and it makes me cautiously optimistic
item.itunes:title: AMD might finally be bringing its most important gaming CPU upgrade to laptops, and it makes me cautiously optimistic
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
AMD's proprietary 3D V-cache is perhaps one of the most important CPU innovations of recent times, and anyone who has been remotely interested in processors knows that already. It's one of AMD's biggest tangible advantages in gaming over competitors right now, and it has been for a while, especially with Team Red steadily refining the formula with every generation.

Now, it looks like AMD could be preparing to bring that same advantage to its next generation of mobile processors. If the reports are to be believed, it could have much bigger implications for gaming laptops for many, many years to come by addressing one of the biggest limitations holding back laptop gaming. Here's why I think the new mobile X3D processors could be the upgrade laptop gamers have been waiting for.

The Ryzen X3D advantage is undeniable, and has been so for years

The 3D V-cache made AMD the default choice for gaming systems

Before I delve into what AMD could be planning for the next generation of mobile chips, it's worth understanding the advantage the 3D V-Cache offers. The most straightforward way to do so is to just compare each X3D chip with its non-X3D counterpart.

The Ryzen 7 5800X3D was the first commercial processor to debut AMD's 3D V-Cache technology in 2022, and counter-intuitively, was about 7% slower than the 5800X in single-threaded workloads and tied with it in multithreaded performance. The real advantage of the first-gen 3D V-Cache, however, was in gaming workloads.

Featuring a total L3 cache size of 96MB, the chip delivered a 15% uplift over the 5800X in TechSpot's 2022 benchmark across 41 titles, while 1% lows improved by an even more impressive 22%. In 1440p performance, where performance is more GPU-limited, the advantage went down to 9% versus the 5800X.

The Ryzen 7 7800X3D continued that trend as expected, averaging 11% more performance than the 7700X in their 2023 benchmark of 12 titles. The third generation, however, was the one to knock it out of the park, with the 9800X3D averaging a staggering 30% faster performance than the 9700X in TechSpot's testing, with some games even showing gains up to 45%.

What should be of great interest to OEMs is that the X3D chips can deliver substantially more gaming performance per watt, and some of the generations achieve that while drawing less power than their non-X3D counterparts. Look no further than the 5800X3D, which, despite having the same 105W TDP as the 5800X, consumes 15% less total system power in comparable workloads.

AMD is resurrecting a 4-year-old CPU, and it exposes some uncomfortable truths about the PC industry

Did they accidentally make AM4 too good?

8
By  Samarveer Singh

The go-to chips for desktop gaming might be coming to laptops

Team Red might just make AMD CPUs the default choice for gaming laptops

AMD has already, in the past, experimented with bringing the 3D V-Cache to gaming laptops, first with the Ryzen 9 7945HX3D and more recently with the Ryzen 9 9955HX3D. The latter uses AMD's second-generation 3D V-Cache tech and is the company's incumbent flagship gaming processor.

The rumors suggest that AMD might've just been getting started all this time. A recent report citing a prominent Chinese tipster, named "Golden Pig Upgrade Pack" claimed on Weibo (a popular social media channel in China) that AMD is preparing another X3D-equipped mobile processor, potentially a Ryzen 7 9800HX3D. The rumored chip would reportedly feature eight Zen 5 cores, 16 threads, and 96MB of L3 cache, with mass production allegedly planned for the Q4 2026 and a possible CES 2027 launch.

But there's a catch, as there has always been

The market has not been kind to consumers when it comes to computing

Putting aside the excitement of another flagship mobile chip release for a moment, the last fourteen months in the consumer technology space has shown just how unkind the economy can be to consumers, mostly owing to the DRAM crisis, which has driven up the total bill of materials up by a considerable margin when it comes to any device that relies on DDR5 memory.

Every mobile X3D chip thus far has been a 16-core flagship locked to a handful of laptops in the range of $2,500 to $5,000, and on Prime Day last year, TechRadar found only five laptops equipped with the Ryzen 9 9955HX3D, with every single one retailing above the $2,300 mark. Right now, the most affordable laptop that comes with a Ryzen 9 9955HX3D can be priced as high as $2,799.

Fortunately enough, there's space for some measured optimism here. Golden Pig Upgrade Pack also claimed that AMD may not lock the new chip to a specific GPU tier as it has done so in the past, which means that OEMs may be able to exercise greater flexibility when coupling the new rumored flagship chip.

This essentially means that a broader category of laptops, across mid-range and upper mid-range, might also see the chip alongside budget GPUs. Given the state of the PC hardware economy, it seems like the prudent thing to do if AMD wants to see any serious market penetration when it comes to the new generation of X3D mobile chips. It most certainly is a better strategy than confining the chip to flagship hardware configurations. However, the ultimate decision of how and where it's implemented will come down heavily to OEMs.

4 scenarios where a Ryzen X3D CPU might be the worst choice

Despite the fame, Ryzen X3D CPUs might be a bad investment for you

24
By  Tanveer Singh

Great hardware, possibly unfortunate timing?

Every great innovation in the PC hardware landscape seems to be arriving at the worst possible time. AMD's mobile X3D chips and their (possible) decision to not lock them to flagship laptops could genuinely change laptop gaming, but whether consumers actually benefit may eventually come down to how much OEMs are willing to compromise on margins. The economic landscape may change, though, and as of now, though, it's reasonable to be cautiously optimistic.

item.itunes:title: Start your homelab with just these 4 containers, not the 20-container checklist everyone recommends

item.itunes:summary:
Most homelab guides hand you a 20+ container checklist to start with. The initial setup is usually the easy part; configuring and maintaining it is the real task that comes later. And most beginners get frustrated and drop the whole idea.

The growth of a homelab should be personal to you and not based on someone else’s stack list. I have been hosting my own services for more than a year now. Whenever someone asks me where to start, I recommend four containers to get started and increase when they need it, and not because somebody suggested it

Portainer makes Docker much easier to understand

You don't need to learn Docker — you need this instead

Whether you are starting with bare metal or a hypervisor, Docker is the most common choice for deploying a service. It is the easiest way to deploy a self-hosted service. But for a beginner, Docker may look like a complex tech stack. Because standalone Docker executes everything on the command line, and honestly, it does look abstract: the containers, images, volumes, and more. Enter Portainer.

Portainer is a Docker management tool. It visualizes everything that happens on the command line. Portainer was the only container I deployed manually via the command line. The whole process of deploying and managing containers becomes a minute’s job.

For deploying, you need to pick the Docker Compose file from the service’s documentation, paste it into Portainer’s Stack, and just press a button to deploy it. After that, all the information you need to manage the container is already there. More importantly, Portainer helps you understand Docker better, i.e., what each container actually consists of.

Portainer

Turns Docker's command-line complexity into a point-and-click dashboard you can actually understand.

See at Official Site

AdGuard Home gives your entire network an immediate upgrade

Ad blocking was never the real reason to install it

Every other guide will tell you to install an ad blocker, usually Pi-hole. I even went with Pi-hole because I wanted network-wide ad blocking. But within a few weeks, I was so deep into it that I learned about encrypted upstream, compared multiple DNS servers, and discovered native recursive DNS resolution. In the end, I settled on AdGuard Home (AGH) with Quad9 DoH.

One DNS tool did what two containers couldn't, and I'm not going back to Pi-hole

The simpler stack was there all along. I didn't upgrade, I removed.

10
By  Shekhar Vaidya

I won’t go deep into each decision; otherwise, this list will turn into a feature. But let me explain a little bit more about my current setup. AGH, along with network-wide ad blocking, monitors network activity, filters each request from each device, and tells me what each device is talking to. And by "network-wide," I mean one implementation on my dual-WAN router as a default DNS server so every device under that network uses it automatically.

You might be thinking, "I already use an ad-blocking extension on my browser and an app on my phone, so why AGH?" Fair question. First, you need to install those extensions and apps on each device. Second, a browser extension only filters ads after they reach the browser, but DNS-based services like AdGuard Home and Pi-hole block them at the DNS level, before they even reach your device.

AdGuard Home

Network-wide ad blocking that quietly teaches you DNS along the way.

See at Github

Jellyfin gives your homelab something you actually want to use

The moment your homelab stops being a hobby and starts being useful

This one container should be the reason why you even thought of getting into homelabbing. For me, it was Jellyfin, so I am suggesting it. But for you, it can be something you already have in mind. It can be a Google Photos alternative like Immich or a self-hosted file-sharing service like Nextcloud. The options are endless, and it totally depends on your use case.

I run my whole media server on a business laptop with no graphics card, and it still transcodes

Turns out the graphics card was optional.

3
By  Shekhar Vaidya

For me, Jellyfin made my homelab a self-hosted media server. It helped me organize my media files and stream them to my family. Not only that, but it also taught me about storage, permissions, volumes, transcoding, networking, and client access. I repurposed an 8-year-old business laptop as my home server (Core i5-6300U, 12GB RAM, and 256GB SSD), so it was a broader lesson for me.

A homelab becomes much more motivating when at least one service solves a problem you care about.

Jellyfin
iOS compatible
Yes
Android compatible
Yes

A self-hosted media server that gives your homelab an actual reason to exist.

See at Jellyfin Jellyfin 12 (RC5)

Uptime Kuma tells you when something goes wrong

The container that stops you from adding a fifth

In the beginning, I mentioned starting a homelab is easy; managing it is the tough job, and this one lightweight container helps you ease the process a little. Sooner or later, you will realize that self-hosted services can stop working without you immediately noticing. This is the harsh truth: a container like Jellyfin can be down for hours without you even noticing.

Uptime Kuma solves that, to some extent. It is a monitoring layer for checking whether the hosted services are reachable. It pings services at regular intervals to check uptime. I always recommend running the monitoring layer on separate infrastructure to cover the blind spots, but in the beginning it doesn’t matter as much.

There are many more monitoring tools available, such as Datadog, Grafana, and Prometheus, but those are advanced tools, and for a beginner homelab, those are overkill. An uptime monitoring tool shows that running a service isn't the same as operating a service. With just this one tiny layer, it rounds out the starting four.

Uptime Kuma
Key highlights
Open-source monitor

A lightweight monitor that tells you the moment something breaks, before anyone else notices.

See at Github

Everything else can wait

A four-container homelab you understand is a better starting point than a 20-container homelab you copied.

Each of the four containers has its own dedicated job. One helps you manage the homelab, one improves your network, one gives you something useful to actually use, and finally, the last one helps you keep track of everything.

These four aren’t a compromise; they’re sufficient to start with. You aren’t supposed to deploy a service just because you saw it on somebody’s stack. As your needs grow, you can explore others, but that should be a choice, not a necessity.

item.title: HP unveils the world's thinnest Nvidia RTX Spark laptops for professionals and gamers alike
item.itunes:title: HP unveils the world's thinnest Nvidia RTX Spark laptops for professionals and gamers alike
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • OmniBook Ultra 16 is an ultra-thin laptop with 1 petaflop AI, up to 128GB RAM, a 16-ionch 3K OLED, and a 17h battery.
  • OmniBook X14 is an ultra-portable OLED laptop, with a strong thermal design, up to 15h battery, and fast 140W charging.
  • OmniDesk desktop has a compact AI node for continuous background agents and long-running tasks.

One half of making a laptop is giving it the most powerful portable hardware on the market; the other half is squeezing all of that into an extremely thin shell. Fortunately, HP seems to have struck the right balance, as it has just announced the world's thinnest RTX Spark laptops. These allow people to tap into on-board AI without sacrificing portability.

HP reveals the OmniBook Ultra 16 for the working professional

It's a strong piece of kit

Credit: HP

The real star of HP's announcements is the OmniBook Ultra 16. We're looking at a laptop designed for heavy-duty AI programming and creative projects, with 128GB of memory and 1 petaflop of AI performance.

That's not to say it's a slacker when it comes to the visuals. As HP puts it, the laptop comes with an impressive screen:

A 16-inch 3K OLED display with VESA DisplayHDR™ True Black 1000 certification is paired with quad speakers powered by smart amplifiers to deliver vibrant visuals, deep contrast and immersive audio experiences for content creation, entertainment, and everyday productivity.

This is all packaged within an ultra-thin shell that maximizes airflow to keep everything cool. It can also run on battery for up to 17 hours and tap into fast-charging technology to reach 50% in 30 minutes.

HP also reveals the HP OmniBook X 14 and the OmniDesk

For those who don't need the most powerful tech

Credit: HP

The OmniBook Ultra 16 wasn't the only announcement that HP made. The company also revealed the HP OmniBook X 14, which offers maximum portability without sacrificing AI tools. It features a brilliant OLED display, an advanced rear thermal architecture, up to 15 hours of battery life, and rapid charging via a 140W USB-C adapter.

Rounding out the lineup is the HP OmniDesk, a compact desktop built for AI performance. It is designed to keep intelligent agents and long-running AI tasks operating continuously in the background, even when the user steps away. The idea is that you can get your AI agents going, go do something else, then come back to see what they've done in the meantime.

Both laptops are slated for release this fall via HP.com and major retailers, with exact pricing details for the entire lineup to follow closer to launch.

Microsoft’s Nvidia RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra will push Windows on Arm further than ever

The tech giant says that the Surface Laptop Ultra's RTX Spark chip has been optimized for Windows 11 with developer and creator workloads in mind.

By  Patrick O'Rourke
